title: Confirmation
hook: the bishop anoints the forehead with perfumed oil: be sealed with the gift of the Holy Spirit

segments.voice: Yesterday, baptism: water three times, in three names. Your line was your first birthday. Did you find the date, or who was there? Day one hundred twenty-seven.

If you've ever been to a Catholic confirmation, you might remember the smell before anything else. The church is full, teenagers in their best clothes lined up in the aisle, families craning to see. One by one they step up to the bishop, often with a sponsor's hand on their shoulder. The bishop dips his thumb in oil and traces a cross on each forehead. And as he gets closer, the whole front of the church smells faintly sweet, like a perfume counter. That smell has a name. Today's word: chrism.
screen: `TEENAGERS IN THE AISLE.` → `A THUMB, A CROSS, A FOREHEAD.` → `THE SMELL OF PERFUME.`

segments.voice: Chrism is olive oil mixed with balsam, a fragrant resin. Once a year, usually in Holy Week, each bishop consecrates it at a special Mass, and it's sent out to every parish. The word comes from the Greek chrisma, an anointing. And it's the same root as Christ, Christos, which means the anointed one. So to be anointed with chrism is, in a sense, to be made like Christ. In the Bible, kings, priests and prophets were anointed with oil to mark them for a task. Confirmation borrows that picture. Where does it come from? In the book of Acts, the people of Samaria hear the Gospel and are baptized. The apostles in Jerusalem send Peter and John, and in the Douay-Rheims, "they laid their hands upon them, and they received the Holy Ghost." Confirmation, Catholics say, continues that moment. As the bishop anoints, he says, in the English form, be sealed with the gift of the Holy Spirit. Sealed, like wax pressed with a signet ring: a mark that says this belongs to someone. The Catholic Church teaches confirmation completes baptism and strengthens a person to live the faith in public. Tradition names seven gifts of the Spirit, drawn from Isaiah: wisdom, understanding, counsel, fortitude, knowledge, piety and fear of the Lord. The timing differs. In Eastern churches, including Eastern Catholics and the Orthodox, the priest anoints babies right after baptism; they call it chrismation. In the Latin Church, it's usually given years later, or to adults at Easter. Many choose a saint's name to take with them.
screen: `OLIVE OIL AND BALSAM.` · `CHRISMA: THE SAME ROOT AS CHRIST.` · `HANDS LAID ON IN SAMARIA.` · `SEVEN GIFTS OF THE SPIRIT.` · then, large: `SEALED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: ask for one gift. Settle, and breathe. Listen to the seven again, slowly: wisdom, understanding, counsel, fortitude, knowledge, piety, fear of the Lord. Fortitude is courage that lasts. Counsel is knowing what to do. Piety is a warm love for God. Which one do you need this week? Pick one. If you pray, you can ask the Holy Spirit for it by name. If you don't, just hold it as a hope, the thing you'd want to be marked with. The bell holds the time.
Chrism. Olive oil and balsam, blessed by the bishop, from the same Greek root as Christ. The oil of confirmation. Today's word.
Your line: sealed. Today, when you need your one gift, touch your forehead for a second and remember you're marked, not alone. Day one hundred twenty-seven.

howItsDone: In the Latin Church most Catholics are confirmed as young people by the bishop, who anoints their foreheads with chrism; Eastern Catholics and the Orthodox receive chrismation as babies right after baptism.

fork.reveal: Peter and John go down, and "they laid their hands upon them, and they received the Holy Ghost." Catholics see confirmation in that moment.

original.note: Greek: an anointing, or the oil used for it. Christos, the anointed one, comes from the same root.

trapdoor: what you thought: a graduation from religion class.
what it means: a sacrament that completes baptism, sealing a person with the Holy Spirit through chrism and the bishop's hand.
what a scholar hears: chrisma and Christos share a root; the rite looks back to Acts 8, and East and West give it at different ages.

notes: The confirmation formula 'Be sealed with the Gift of the Holy Spirit' is the ICEL English (copyrighted); used without quotation marks as a description of the words said. Latin: Accipe signaculum doni Spiritus Sancti. Confirm acceptable.
Acts 8:17 DR wording — verify against a Challoner text.
Chrism consecrated at the Chrism Mass, usually Holy Thursday morning or earlier in Holy Week. Confirm.
Seven gifts: from Isaiah 11:2–3 in the Septuagint/Vulgate (piety added). Listed with CCC 1831's names. Confirm.
Confirmation names: a custom, not required. Latin Church age varies by country (US: roughly 7–16). Confirm phrasing.
